title: DeepSpeed-FastGen: High-throughput Text Generation for LLMs via MII and DeepSpeed-Inference
technique: Dynamic SplitFuse: decompose long prompts into chunks and compose them with decode tokens to fill a fixed per-forward-pass token budget; blocked KV cache

optimized_metrics.evidence: When systems treat them as distinct phases, generation will be preempted by prompt processing that risks breaking the service level agreements (SLAs).
DeepSpeed-FastGen will consume tokens from incoming prompts at a rate that permits fast ongoing generation while adding tokens to the system that increase system utilization
providing lower latency and higher throughput streaming generation to all clients as compared to other state-of-the-art serving systems
providing lower latency and higher throughput streaming generation to all clients as compared to other state-of-the-art serving systems

headline_claim.text: up to 2.3x higher effective throughput, 2x lower latency on average, and up to 3.7x lower (token-level) tail latency, compared to state-of-the-art systems like vLLM

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Two key metrics for production readiness are throughput (measured in requests per second) and latency (the responsiveness of each request).
metric_definitions.notes: requests/s, measured as total requests / end-to-end time of experiment

metric_definitions.definition_quote: The resulting latency of each request is measured at the endpoint and throughput is measured by the end-to-end time to complete the experiment.
define the SLA for prompt latency as (tokens in prompt)/512 seconds (=512 tokens/s).
metric_definitions.locator: §4.1.2 (formula garbled in PDF: 'tokens in prompt / 512 seconds')
metric_definitions.notes: first-token SLA scales with prompt length: 512 prompt tokens/s

metric_definitions.definition_quote: we set the SLA for generation latency on the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) to 2, 4, or 6 tokens/sec.
metric_definitions.notes: per-request token generation rate, EMA-smoothed; basis 'human reading speed'

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Requests that adhere to these SLAs are deemed successful, and the throughput of these successful requests is referred to as effective throughput.
metric_definitions.notes: unit: requests/s of SLA-meeting requests (queries/s); peak of effective-throughput curve is 'optimal serving point'

metric_definitions.term_as_written: token-level tail latency / P95 generation latency
metric_definitions.definition_quote: Figure 5 displays the P50, P90, and P95 latencies of the generation processes.
metric_definitions.notes: '(token-level) tail latency' in the abstract; per-token generation latency distribution, exact unit (per-token vs per-request) not strictly defined

slo_spec: Effective-throughput SLA: prompt latency <= (prompt tokens)/512 s; generation EMA rate >= 2, 4 or 6 tokens/s (human reading speed); successful request must meet both.
load_regime: closed-loop client sweep (1-32 concurrent clients, 512 requests), throughput-latency curves; also 16-replica load balancing
tradeoff_acknowledged: Argues balance between throughput and latency; vLLM preemption of generation for prompts causes P90/P95 latency spikes (the trade-off they avoid).
workloads: synthetic: normal-distributed prompt/generation lengths, averages 1200/2600 prompt and 128/60 generation, 30% variance
extractor_notes: Blog-style paper. 'latency' for 'throughput-latency curves' is per-request end-to-end latency; generation latency definition in Fig 5/7 is per-token latency percentile. 'Effective throughput' = goodput but in requests/s. Primary design metric is a per-forward-pass token budget; throughput/latency claims are evaluation outcomes. Tail percentiles P90/P95 only for generation latency. | TAIL AUDIT 2026-10-06: TBT tail stat -> n/a (metric targeted, percentile only reported)

tail_audit.correction: Demote TBT P95 'objective' to reported. Its SLA is prompt latency bound + EMA token rate >= 2/4/6 tok/s (no percentile).

load_class_quote: we instantiate multiple clients (ranging from 1 to 32) concurrently and send requests (512 in total) to the server (§4.1.1; closed-loop client-count sweep, not an arrival-rate process)
